🚀 feature request

 Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/forms.

 Description

In complex forms it can be necessary to react to value changes to update some state (e.g. when some JSON/YAML configuration can be shown both in a JSON/YAML editor ("advanced view") and individual form controls and they need to be synced up). However, checkboxes or select inputs are inherently different from text inputs in one specific way: frequency of value changes, with the latter receiving significantly more.

Therefore it would be nice if individual form controls could easily be debounced such that their valueChange emits less frequently. This is opposed to debouncing the entire FormGroup's valueChange which would unnecessarily debounce these other controls as well.

I maintain a library, ngqp which uses the forms infrastructure to wire up form controls with query parameters, and there I have this feature implemented and got the inspiration from to make this feature request.

 Describe the solution you'd like

An addition to AbstractControlOptions such that this can be done:

 

 Describe alternatives you've considered

Technically this can already be achieved by splitting the valueChange observable using distinctUntilChanged etc. and merging it back, but that requires quite a bit of effort. If this could be a configuration on the form control itself, however, users would have a simple, declarative solution.

---

This request is related to and possibly a duplicate of 19705, but that request is specifically about template-driven forms while I am focusing on reactive forms here.
kept_issues.body:
# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/forms.

### Description

In complex forms it can be necessary to react to value changes to update some state (e.g. when some JSON/YAML configuration can be shown both in a JSON/YAML editor ("advanced view") and individual form controls and they need to be synced up). However, checkboxes or select inputs are inherently different from text inputs in one specific way: frequency of value changes, with the latter receiving significantly more.

Therefore it would be nice if individual form controls could easily be debounced such that their valueChange emits less frequently. This is opposed to debouncing the entire FormGroup's valueChange which would unnecessarily debounce these other controls as well.

I maintain a library, [ngqp](https://github.com/TNG/ngqp) which uses the forms infrastructure to wire up form controls with query parameters, and there I have this feature implemented and got the inspiration from to make this feature request.

### Describe the solution you'd like

An addition to AbstractControlOptions such that this can be done:

```
formBuilder.control('', {debounceTime: 100});
```


### Describe alternatives you've considered

Technically this can already be achieved by splitting the valueChange observable using distinctUntilChanged etc. and merging it back, but that requires quite a bit of effort. If this could be a configuration on the form control itself, however, users would have a simple, declarative solution.

---

This request is related to and possibly a duplicate of #19705, but that request is specifically about template-driven forms while I am focusing on reactive forms here.
kept_issues.title: Debounce individual form controls

 Relevant Package
 
 This feature request is for @angular/localize (and possibly @angular/cli, @angular/compiler-cli)

 Description
 
@petebacondarwin This is a follow-up feature request based on your comment to check if there are plans or progress on "runtime translation" as you describe below, without having to rely on www.locl.app (which is not available yet anyway).

"This is what we mean in the core Angular framework as runtime translation. But please not that the final outcome of this is effectively the same as translation at compile time. The translation happens only once; if you want to change the language at runtime then you must restart the whole application (e.g. via a reload). This has the benefit of allowing the project to deploy a single distributable with numerous translation files, which is helpful in a small number of use cases where you do not want to generate all the different translations up front."

To give you a scenario, we are building Ionic apps using Angular so the "allowing the project to deploy a single distributable with numerous translation files" would be a great benefit to us. We are OK with reloading the app, although some built-in way to do this as the app bootstraps (or soon after) would be great to avoid workarounds etc..

 Describe the solution you'd like
 
A single build/bundle with the ability to switch locales at runtime via a seamless reload of the app. Seamless means a way to reload the correct locale app at the early possible time based on either device info, user input, and/or locale storage (realizing that would be app specific code but some built-in hook would be great).

Since we already do the translations "up front" via xliff files, some way of hooking into those translations would be awesome. Without know the internals of Angular, a possible design for this is a single build in /dist with the translations (originating from the xliff files) distributed to dist/ , with the /dist root defaulting to the sourceLocale in angular.json. Possibly there is an index.html file in each dist/ that when requested by the web browser gets the main bundles from /dist but "swaps" the locale code from the current dist/ folder request. I could be way off here :).

 Describe alternatives you've considered
 
We will have to distribute all full locale builds on the device and manually reload via code (don't have a sample of this just yet). Really (really, really, ...) do not want to us ngx-translate.

🚀 feature request

 Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/platform-browser/animations

 Description
To make our app start as quickly as possible, particularly on mobile, I've done a bunch of work to minimize initial bundle size. One of the approaches I'm using is async imports (eg import('../foo/foo.module').then(m => m.FooModule)) shortly after the app is loaded, for logic that isn't absolutely required for initial load + first render.

While we use angular animations extensively (because it's awesome!), we don't need it for first page view (relying on CSS animations for the first few seconds). It is currently not possible to move the BrowserAnimationsModule import to a different module from where BrowserModule is imported - because BrowserAnimationModule exports BrowserModule, and the BrowserModule constructor requires that BrowserModule hasn't been loaded in a parent injector. Also, angular won't start if BrowserModule isn't imported by the root module.

I would like the ability to delay load BrowserAnimationsModule, and I think this would be a useful ability for anyone working to speed initial load.

The easiest repro is to create a new project using ng new --strict --minimal. Next, ng build --prod gives me a main bundle size of 187kB.

If I'm going to use @angular/animations in my app, I am currently required to import BrowserAnimationsModule in the root module:

 

Just doing this increases the main bundle to 258 kB (+71kB or +38%).

 Describe the solution you'd like

I'd like to be able to initialize the BrowserAnimationsModule shortly after app load, and have animations work after that point:

await delay(1000);
import('@angular/platform-browser/animations').then(m => m.BrowserAnimationsModule );

This will probably require that the BrowserAnimationsModule no longer re-export BrowserModule.

 Describe alternatives you've considered
The current required configuration works, it just adds unnecessary size to the initial bundle.

I did try directly importing BROWSER_ANIMATIONS_PROVIDERS (which would get around the BrowserModule re-import check), but I couldn't access them.

Another alternative would be to fork the angular code and try to create a new version of BrowserAnimationsModule that doesn't have these limitations, but I haven't gotten desparate enough for that. We'll see what the Angular team thinks about this proposal.
kept_issues.title: Make BrowserAnimationsModule delay-loadable

🚀 feature request
Provide a way to check for updates and activate them before the main AppModule is bootstrapped.

 Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/service-worker

 Description
Currently, if we use the service worker module(which we want to use in order to support offline mode) we have no choice but always serve a cached(potentially outdated) version when a user opens our app. And only then we can check for updates in the background.

What we want is to check for updates before bootstrapping the app and if there are any then first activate them and only after that bootstrap an app. We want to be sure that a user starts her working day with a fresh version of our app (if for example there was an overnight update).

We considered force page reload and showing a prompt for a user to activate a new version but that would not be the best UX choice in our scenarios(we do updates a couple of times daily).

 Describe the solution you'd like
Provide an API to access service worker's checkForUpdate, available and activateUpdate properties outside of a module/service so it can be done in main.ts.

 Describe alternatives you've considered
We can't remove the service worker since we want offline support.
We can't force refresh as it's a bad UX for us(we can on navigation between routes but that would be too late)
We can't show prompt as it will appear almost every morning for the user.

We consider showing a spinner in app.component until we make all checks through the ServiceWorkerModule as an alternative but that would be a waste of the device's(in case of mobile) resources to parse and execute all JS to then find out it's not needed.

🚀 feature request

 Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/core.

 Description
Right now, the changes detection cycle:
- updates all input bindings, gradually populating SimpleChanges object
- fires ngOnChanges with the built SimpleChanges, allowing to process the changes collectively

As far as I can tell, there's no documented order of input bindings update. It means that before I have a chance to process changes as a whole, the change processing fires input updates in an order I don't know - and even if I can figure it out from the sources and control it, I still can't rely on it if it's not documented.

This becomes a problem in the following scenario:
- I have one input affecting the list of available items
- I have another input changing the currently selected item, but ignoring the new value if it's outside the range of available items
- in the same change detection cycle, I change available items from collection without item X to a collection with item X and change the currently selected item to X
- the input processing system decides to first attempt to choose X as selected item (but X is not among available items), then update the list of available items (only then making X available)

 Describe the solution you'd like
I'd like to propose a new lifecycle hook: ngBeforeChanges/ngOnChanging. This hook would be called after input changes have been determined, but before inputs would be processed.

In this lifecycle hook, the user could:
- access information about input changes, so that they could process these collectively
- prevent updating certain inputs, usually done when the user handled the input themself
- an additional method for eager processing input would be nice (basically, assign the incoming input to the corresponding value and prevent the input)

This allows finer control over input processing order. For example, in the described scenario I could hook to ngOnChanging, I could do something like:
 

Additionally, it allows simultaneous processing of inputs before they are processed individually. It can be used for optimising updates when some relatively expensive processing is triggered by updating either of several values.
 

Interactions with existing functionality
We might want to consider the intended use of input prevention:
- default input processing is meant to be prevented only if the user processed the input themselves
- input processing may be prevented because the user processed the input themselves or refused to process it altogether

As of now, I can only think of reasonable scenarios when default input processing is prevented because user processes it instead. In fact, outright refusing to process inputs might go against the expectations of what inputs are meant to do.

If we assume that all inputs are meant to be processed - some just may be pre-processed by users - I'd keep ngOnChanges the way it works now. I.e. SimpleChanges object contains all the changes - user-prevented and default-processed alike - and doesn't differentiate between them. That's the option I lean towards - I intend user pre-processing to enhance the input processing in general, not to make it a completely new thing.

If we allow refusing to process inputs, we might want to reflect it in some way or another in SimpleChanges object, whether by adding something like "isCancelled" property to SimpleChange or removing the change altogether.

Implementation notes
Judging by the sources I've seen earlier but can't find now (I think the file was called provider.ts or something similar, and there are lots of providers), the inputs processing right now interleaves input processing and SimpleChanges building (i.e. there's a method that updates bound input and returns a new simple changes object).

If gather changes + optionally call ngOnChanging + apply non-prevented changes + optionally call ngOnChanges method is significantly more expensive than current apply and gather changes + optionally call ngOnChanges, maybe we could opt for the current input processing for directives that don't implement ngOnChanging. Hopefully, the cost of checking for ngOnChanging implementation is negligible.

 Describe alternatives you've considered
One workaround I tried before was a mechanism for buffering changes when receiving input, then processing these changes in ngOnChanges(...). It got pretty messy, however, especially considering the fact that same component value could be changed via external Input or via internal Output (it was bound to inner input value).

Possibly cleaner workaround I just came up with is having separate dummy Input values - separate from the main values - and process these in ngOnChanges(...). This should allow separating Input()-variables handling (e.g. to control inputs processing orders) and not polluting the processing of core variables.

So if I e.g. have availableValues: any[] and selectedValue: any properties with all their processing, then I'd add @Input('availableValues') inputAvailableValues: any[]; and @Input('selectedValue') inputSelectedValue: any;, then I'd process these inputs in ngOnChanges.

Not sure how well it works if I have @Input() someValue; in a base class then @Input('someValue') inputSomeValue in a child class. If the latter declaration completely overrides the former, I guess it would make the workaround relatively clean and effective.

Still, having an ngBeforeChange/ngOnChanging hook would make the dummy input variables unnecessary and also provide much more intuitive place to handle incoming inputs. I at least wouldn't have wasted hours on trying to find a reasonably clean and properly working solution to the inputs asynchronism problem.

Another option could be specifying the order of processing inputs manually, e.g. in the @Input() dectorator (with 0 being a default order). However, it's not as flexible and doesn't cover the scenario of one-time expensive processing of simultaneously updated values.
kept_issues.title: ngBeforeChanges/ngOnChanging and preventing further Input processing

### Relevant Package

@angular/compiler-cli


### Description
@clydin talked to @alxhub in the past to introduce something like `getModuleDependencies`/ `getSourcefileDepedencies` which would go along `getResourceDependencies` which was landed via angular/angular#38048.

NGTSC adds dependencies between files which is currently not being handled because such dependencies are not created via import/exports statements. This relation between these files is not known to `@ngtools/webpack` and `Webpack`, which causes updated files not to be emitted when doing change. (https://github.com/angular/angular-cli/issues/18707, https://github.com/angular/angular-cli/issues/19063, https://github.com/angular/angular/issues/39178)
 
One such scenario is the reversed dependency added by from `app.component` to `app.module` via the `directives` metadata.

```.ts
class AppComponent {
    constructor() {
        this.title = 'material-test';
    }
}
AppComponent.ɵfac = function AppComponent_Factory(t) { return new (t || AppComponent)(); };
AppComponent.ɵcmp = _angular_core__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_0__["ɵɵdefineComponent"]({ type: AppComponent, selectors: [["app-root"]], decls: 2, vars: 0, consts: [["matInput", ""]], template: function AppComponent_Template(rf, ctx) { if (rf & 1) {
        _angular_core__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_0__["ɵɵelementStart"](0, "mat-form-field");
        _angular_core__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_0__["ɵɵelement"](1, "input", 0);
        _angular_core__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_0__["ɵɵelementEnd"]();
    } }, directives: [_angular_material_form_field__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_1__["MatFormField"], _angular_material_input__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_2__["MatInput"]], styles: ["\n/*# sourceMappingURL=data:application/json;base64,eyJ2ZXJzaW9uIjozLCJzb3VyY2VzIjpbXSwibmFtZXMiOltdLCJtYXBwaW5ncyI6IiIsImZpbGUiOiJzcmMvYXBwL2FwcC5jb21wb25lbnQuY3NzIn0= */"] });
/*@__PURE__*/ (function () { _angular_core__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_0__["ɵsetClassMetadata"](AppComponent, [{
        type: _angular_core__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_0__["Component"],
        args: [{
                selector: 'app-root',
                templateUrl: './app.component.html',
                styleUrls: ['./app.component.css']
            }]
    }], null, null); })();
```

The means that when doing a change to `app.module`, `app.component` should also emitted. However, this is not the case because Webpack is only aware of the one way relation that `app.module` is a dependant of `app.component` and not the two way relation.

Related and needed to resolve https://github.com/angular/angular-cli/issues/18707 and the month the dependency tree is built using the following code https://github.com/angular/angular-cli/blob/677f6007268c534982c748faeebccb369cb4bc64/packages/ngtools/webpack/src/loader.ts#L64-L107

### Describe the solution you'd like
NGTSC should provide an API, that returns the dependencies of a given source file.

# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package

This feature request is for `@angular/elements`.

### Description

When using `@angular/elements`, outputs are converted to `CustomEvents`:
https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/eb9eebbb45352da6000560ee0988d9d59dce1254/packages/elements/src/create-custom-element.ts#L225-L228

There is no way of listening to the custom events from a grand parent element or component because these custom events don't bubble as the `bubbles` option is set to `false` here:

https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/eb9eebbb45352da6000560ee0988d9d59dce1254/packages/elements/src/utils.ts#L55-L70

It would be nice to figure out a way of listening to custom events in grand parent elements.

### Use Case
The app loads dynamic markdown content. This markdown is processed with a third party library like [Marked](https://github.com/markedjs/marked) where we add a special link handler that replaces links with our custom elements (using Angular Elements). These elements trigger custom events that we want to handle in the parent component (the one that loaded the markdown).

The general idea is that we can let a 3rd party (non-Angular) library control the DOM and inject our Angular Elements but we want to keep communicating with these elements without having to dispatch bubbling events manually or using an indirection like a provider or state management etc...

### Solutions

#### Solution A

1. Create a new `CustomEventEmitter` where we can configure `bubbles` and `cancelable`: 
```ts
new CustomEventEmitter({bubbles: true, cancelable: false})
```
_We can't use `EventEmitter` because `bubbles` and `cancelable` will be simply ignored and confusing when not using Angular elements_

2. Change `ComponentNgElementStrategy` in order to handle `CustomEventEmitter` differently instead of merging all emitters:
https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/eb9eebbb45352da6000560ee0988d9d59dce1254/packages/elements/src/component-factory-strategy.ts#L50

3. Change `createCustomElement` in order to handle `bubbles` and `cancelable`:
https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/eb9eebbb45352da6000560ee0988d9d59dce1254/packages/elements/src/create-custom-element.ts#L225-L228

4. Change `createCustomEvent` to allow the control of `bubbles` and `cancelable`:
https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/eb9eebbb45352da6000560ee0988d9d59dce1254/packages/elements/src/utils.ts#L55-L70

5. [OPTIONAL] Should we deprecate `EventEmitter` usage with Angular elements? Allowing both can be confusing.

#### Solution B

Create a new `CustomEventEmitter` which is an `EventEmitter` of type `EventEmitter<{bubbles?: boolean, cancelable?: boolean, detail?: T}>` so every event can have a different bubbling strategy... but that would be a surprising behavior so I am not a big fan of this one.

#### Contribution
I'll be more than happy to contribute with a PR if the solution is suitable.

### Workaround
Trigger the event manually:
```ts
elementRef.nativeElement.dispatchEvent('myCustomEvent', {bubbles: true, detail: 'data'})
```

### Somewhat related issues
https://github.com/angular/angular/issues/2296
kept_issues.title: Allow dispatch of bubbling custom events when using `@angular/elements`

Important note: this ticket just describes possible ideas on how to make Forms code more tree-shakable. There are no specific actions planned/needed at this point.

Currently a lot of logic in Forms is stored in classes (such as AbstractControl, FormControl, FormGroup, FormArray, Validators, etc). The code in these classes is not tree-shakable by Terser. Closure can tree-shake unused class methods, but it requires advanced optimization mode turned on (which may or may not be enabled for different apps for various reasons).

There are some PRs that add more logic (util methods) into AbstractControl-based classes (see 27222, 34210 and also related issues 27171, 34186). Adding more methods into AbstractControl-based classes would lead to additional payload size even if applications do not use them. It'd be great to have a way to add this kind of helpers/utils in a tree-shakable way (otherwise we won't be able to include them into the Forms code).

One possible solution to consider is creating standalone functions that would take the necessary controls as arguments are perform some actions inside, for example with the moveControl function (from 27222) that might look like:

 

Note: there is a lot of consideration that should be taken into account (such as backwards-compatibility, DX, API consistency and ergonomics, etc) before creating any helper methods and more research/discussion is needed (when this work is prioritized).

# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package
<!-- Can you pin-point one or more @angular/* packages the are relevant for this feature request? -->
<!-- ✍️edit: --> This feature request is for @angular/core


### Description
<!-- ✍️--> Improve component encapsulation while removing cluttering of `NgModule`


### Describe the solution you'd like
<!-- ✍️--> Inside the `@Component` metadata, add the key: `declarations`, that key should accept an array of components, similar to the api used in `@NgModule`.  



```typescript
@Component({
    selector: 'nz-header',
    template: `
        <header>
            <nz-nav></nz-nav>
        </header>
    `,
    declarations: [NavComponent]
})
export class HeaderComponent { ... }
```


### Describe alternatives you've considered
<!-- ✍️--> Yes, Feature module and dynamic components

### Long description

One of the programming concepts that guides us as developers is encapsulation.  
The ability to expose what we need to expose as public, and to hide the rest as private.  
Consider the following components, module.  

Our module `AppModule` contains the following components:

- `HeaderComponent`
  - `NavComponent`
- `FooterComponent`

`HeaderComponent` is placing the `NavComponent`, and the `NavComponent` will be used **only** in the `HeaderComponent`

The `NavComponent` is a component that should only be used in the `HeaderComponent` it's like a private implementation of the `HeaderComponent`.  
Encapsulation rules should not expose `NavComponent` to the other components inside our module.  
So the `FooterComponent` should not be able to place the `NavComponent` since it's private to the `HeaderComponent`.  

Currently to declare the structure above our `AppModule` would look like this:

```typescript
@NgModule({
    declarations: [HeaderComponent, NavComponent, FooterComponent]
})
export class AppModule {}
```

this configuration will allow both the `HeaderComponent` and the `FooterComponent` to place the `NavComponent`.  
In my opinion this breaks encapsulation rules and clutters the `NgModule` with a lot of components which should be private.  
The ideal would be that we can declare the module like this:

```typescript
@NgModule({
    declarations: [HeaderComponent, FooterComponent]
})
export class AppModule {}
```

And declare the `HeaderComponent` like this:

```typescript
@Component({
    selector: 'nz-header',
    template: `
        <header>
            <nz-nav></nz-nav>
        </header>
    `,
    declarations: [NavComponent]
})
export class HeaderComponent { ... }
```

And of course not allow the `FooterComponent` to add the selector of the `NavComponent`.

I can arrange a folder for the `HeaderComponent` and arrange in that same folder all the private components that header is using.  

The result will be:
- cleaner `NgModule` with smaller array of components
- Better encapsulation in the components
- Better communication to the team regarding what components they can use and what is hidden

# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/common

### Description
Currently, we do have a lot of syntaxes supported on ngClass. But there's no way to mix up the `[]`, and `{}` syntax. There are scenarios that we will need a ternary operator to choose between two sets of classes dynamically, and there's also chances that we just need one.


### Describe the solution you'd like
I setup a [sample](https://stackblitz.com/edit/angular-ivy-gkhqfc?file=src/app/app.component.html) where I describe the solution I like.

As you can see in there, I am comparing the key name of the object by putting it in square brackets. And when the condition false to any of the class stated, it will be return as a property key name.

```
<hello name="{{ name }}" [ngClass]="{
  [myCheckBox ? italic: underline]: true, 
  red: myCheckBox2, 
  serif: true}">
</hello>

<input type="checkbox" [(ngModel)]="myCheckBox" /> Style
<input type="checkbox" [(ngModel)]="myCheckBox2" /> Colour
```

This is what I have in mind, but it would be cleaner if we can handle it without explicitly putting `true` on it.


### Describe alternatives you've considered
Currently, the workaround for this is to put it on a square bracket array syntax and pass an empty class in case the condition falls to the other condition.
```
<hello name="{{ name }}" [ngClass]="[myCheckBox ? 'italic': 'underline', myCheckBox2 ? 'red' : '', 'serif' ]">
</hello>
```
kept_issues.title: Add support for square, and curly brackets in ngClass

 - a new version starts downloading

# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/service-worker

### Description
We are currently experiencing an issue with a significant percentage of our users using outdated versions of our application. We're not really sure whether they're taking a very long time to update their applications or is it more of a problem with detection of the new version or something else. We don't have enough data to determine whether there is an issue with our service worker implementation, an issue with our application or maybe some edge case in the framework. [Currently](https://angular.io/guide/service-worker-communications) the service worker exposes only the `available` and `activated` events. This gives only a bit of an insight on how does the service worker perform updates on the client side. 

### Describe the solution you'd like
As mentioned before the service worker currently exposes only two events
 - a new version is available to be activated
 - a new version has been activated

Ideally the service would expose some additional events like
 - a new version has been detected to exist (but is not available to use yet)
 - a new version starts downloading
 - a new version finishes downloading

This would allow us to track those events, figure out why is it that some users are taking very long time to get the new version and/or maybe optimise some parts of the flow.

##
_**EDIT(gkalpak)**_
_Related issue: #34397_

kept_issues.body:
# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Packages

This feature request is for `@angular/core` and `@angular/compiler`.

### Description

The object used as context for `TemplateRef` is not accessible from the template; only the values of its keys are. Therefore, it's not possible to

1. easily reference keys of a large object, or
2. pass the whole context to another template reference.

For example, consider the following context.

```ts
const context = { foo: 1, bar: 2, baz: 3, qux: 4 }
```

In order to just print all of these values, it's necessary to write the following template.

```html
                   <!-------------- verbose & error-prone --------------->
<ng-template #tpl1 let-foo="foo" let-bar="bar" let-baz="baz" let-qux="qux">
  {{ foo }}, {{ bar }}, {{ baz }}, {{ qux }}
</ng-template>
```

The list of `let-xxx="xxx"` will just keep increasing with the same mundane boilerplate code as the object grows. 

Furthermore, two such templates won't be easily composable, even though they accept the same kind of context.

```html
                   <!-------------- verbose & error-prone --------------->
<ng-template #tpl2 let-foo="foo" let-bar="bar" let-baz="baz" let-qux="qux">
  Elements: 
  <ng-template
    [ngTemplateOutlet]="tpl1"
    [ngTemplateOutletContext]="{ foo: foo, bar: bar, baz: baz, qux: qux }" 
  >
                               <!-------- verbose & error-prone -------->
</ng-template>
```

Apart from `{ foo: foo, bar: bar, baz: baz, qux: qux }` being equally verbose and error-prone as `let-foo="foo" let-bar="bar" let-baz="baz" let-qux="qux"` (especially since there's almost no type checking for these cases), this will create a new object for every CD cycle (more on that below).

### Describe the solution you'd like

A way to get a hold of the context object itself. Templates in the examples above could be rewritten as follows.

```html
                   <!-- <3 -->
<ng-template #tpl1 let-ctx="*">
  {{ ctx.foo }}, {{ ctx.bar }}, {{ ctx.baz }}, {{ ctx.qux }}
</ng-template>
```

```html
                   <!-- <3 -->
<ng-template #tpl2 let-ctx="*">
  Elements:
  <ng-template
    [ngTemplateOutlet]="tpl1"
    [ngTemplateOutletContext]="ctx"
  >
                            <!--<3-->
</ng-template>
```

The precise syntax doesn't have to be like this, but the `*` symbol should ring a bell from the namespaced import syntax `import * as context from 'context'`. I don't think there's issues about confusion with the microsyntax prefix (`*ngFor`, `*ngIf`) since the asterisk in case of `let-ctx="*"` doesn't come as a prefix, and it's placed in the spot where a variable name can otherwise come in.

An alternative syntax that comes to mind would be using `...` which rings the bell of the spread/rest operator, which is similar in nature to what this proposal tries to achieve.

```html
                   <!--  <3  -->
<ng-template #tpl1 let-ctx="...">
  {{ ctx.foo }}, {{ ctx.bar }}, {{ ctx.baz }}, {{ ctx.qux }}
</ng-template>
```

```html
                   <!--  <3  -->
<ng-template #tpl2 let-ctx="...">
  Elements:
  <ng-template
    [ngTemplateOutlet]="tpl1"
    [ngTemplateOutletContext]="ctx"
  >
</ng-template>
```

Ultimately, the syntax isn't the main point of this proposal and these are just examples. I'd love to see others' take on what looks easiest to write and read, and how to make the intent more intuitive based on existing ES and/or Angular constructs.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Obviously, `$implicit` is the alternative. This _seems_ like a good solution:

```ts
const context = { $implicit: { foo: 1, bar: 2, baz: 3, qux: 4 } } // meh
```

```html
<ng-template #tpl1 let-ctx>
  {{ ctx.foo }}, {{ ctx.bar }}, {{ ctx.baz }}, {{ ctx.qux }}
</ng-template>

<ng-template
  [ngTemplateOutlet]="tpl1"
  [ngTemplateOutletContext]="context"
></ng-template>
```

The problem that arises now is that we've changed our model. If we have an array of `User` objects, now we need an array of `{ $implicit: User }` objects. Wrapping objects to an `$implicit` property is something that we'd have to do only because the view requires so. Changing our model to match the view is not how the whole separation of concerns and the model-view architecture is supposed to work (or at least we try to minimize that). The view should be able to adapt to the model, not the other way around.

Now, one way for the view to adopt to the model is, of course, the following.

```ts
const context = { foo: 1, bar: 2, baz: 3, qux: 4 } // good
```

```html
<ng-template #tpl1 let-ctx>
  {{ ctx.foo }}, {{ ctx.bar }}, {{ ctx.baz }}, {{ ctx.qux }}
</ng-template>

<ng-template
  [ngTemplateOutlet]="tpl1"
  [ngTemplateOutletContext]="{ $implicit: context }"
></ng-template>
                             <!-- mixed feelings -->
```

The issue is that this creates a new object `{ $implicit: context }` in every CD cycle. 

Note that [`NgTemplateOutlet` of `@angular/common` itself was changed to check for equality-by-shape instead of equality-by-reference](https://github.com/angular/angular/commit/685cc26ab2dc7f8d836ec932a43d45edfa0f8e97) because it was such a common use-case to create the object inline in the template. That idea introduces more runtime checks in order to allow this common style.

While the solution works, I'm not sure it was a step in the right direction (I'd like to hear what the author of the commit, @pkozlowski-opensource thinks about it). Apart from introducing the runtime check, I feel like it attempts to patch the problem instead of addressing the root cause: the actual _need_ to create objects inline in the template as opposed to just using them from the code -- which is what this proposal is about. Either way, this proposal is not in conflict with the established runtime check-by-shape, so it's not a breaking change; users who worry about performance can create their own variant `NgTemplateOutlet` which only does a simple check by reference.

----

This mostly seems like job for the compiler, as I don't think it introduces any special changes to the core -- that object is already passed around unchanged, and this proposal “only” allows grabbing the object itself instead of just its keys via `let-localName`.

As usual, “only” is possibly a rabbit hole of issues. I haven't tried to implement this yet, but I will post here if I manage to get a prototype working for the `let-ctx="*"` syntax (it _looks_ as if it's just a matter of treating `*` as a special case and then passing in `context` instead of `context['*']` for it).
kept_issues.title: [Proposal] Allow referencing the whole TemplateRef context object from the template

# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package

@angular/core

### Description

Detaching views is (sometimes) absolutely necessary for good performance.

```html
<item *ngFor="let item of longList" [value]="item"></item>
```

Whenever a single `item` is invalidated (even for a mousemove event), Angular has to check every single `item`. Unless of course they are detached.

But.....**detach() is practically unusable** because it's very, very poorly supported.

Angular Material is perhaps the best-made Angular library and even it breaks if detaching any parent. Example: https://stackblitz.com/edit/angular-nvcgil (expandable area will not expand)

### Describe the solution you'd like

When I detach from change detection, what I really want is to *not to dirty the parent*, not to change how the children operate.

In other words, I want to make the component a "root" for change detection.

AFAIK there is no mechanism to do that currently.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

* Not detaching. The causes poor performance.
* Fixed libraries for detached change detection. But I'm 100% certain the Angular team will refuse my PRs to Angular Material.
* Not using libraries.

It's unfortunate having to choose between using libraries and having performance.
kept_issues.title: Make ChangeDetectorRef#detach() work with most child components

🚀 feature request

 Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/router

 Description
Consider populating the router.config…children array the same for static and lazy loaded routes.

 Describe the solution you'd like

Some developers including myself like to create navigation elements, say for a header component, directly from the router.confg. Everything is already populated in the router config (including custom data and access via a RouteGuard). When using static routes I would normally do something like the following.

 

The code above simply creates an object array called items for the children of a specific route. I am not showing all the detail but just focusing on the children array because these are static routes. The object returned can be anything the developer needs. 

Now when using lazy loaded routes the children array is not available because the routing data is stored in lazy loaded modules that have not been loaded yet. Several people have tried to use the private _loadedConfig property on a route but it gets ugly and you end up with something like this.

 

While this works its not ideal. The obvious issue is that the private _loadedConfig is subject to change without warning in the future because its not part of the public API and this object is not available until some point in the lifecycle that I have not been able to determine yet. 

Now the data that is eventually available in the _loadedConfig is exactly what developers are interested in (path, data, etc.) and it seems to be available even before the lazy modules are loaded. Given this would it be possible to present this information using the normal children array regardless if it’s a static route or a lazy loaded route? In most scenarios developers only care to have access to the route children and its less important that it’s from a static route vs. a lazy loaded route. A Boolean or enumeration could be added that would let the developer know the route static vs lazy if that is important. 

This would mean any code designed to work with the router, config, and children would work with static or lazy loaded routes. The project could start with standard static routes and then later be reconfigured to use lazy routes and any code already in place that leverages the router config would continue to work.

One additional thought would be at webpack/compile time Angular would have access to all the routes regardless if they are static or lazy. Maybe some metadata can be derived from this and used to populate the routes children information at runtime.
 
I know it’s a long shot, but I wanted to suggest the general idea.

Thanks,
Eric
kept_issues.title: Consider populating the router.config…children array the same for static and lazy loaded routes

 Relevant Package

@angular/forms

 Description

Angular forms that have controls with multiple Validator.pattern validators (which sometimes are very large regex strings) are difficult to map to the correct messages.

This can be done by comparing the requiredPattern property which is not ideal for large regex strings on large forms. Instead, we are currently forking the Validator.pattern code for just to set a different "error" than the default value of "pattern".

 Describe the solution you'd like

Extend the Validator.pattern method with an optional parameter that either replaces the pattern key or adds a new property inside of the validation error.

Example:

Validator.pattern( ... , 'my custom error')

would return an error like:

{'my custom error': {'requiredPattern': regexStr, 'actualValue': value}};

or:

{'pattern': {'error': 'my custom error', 'requiredPattern': regexStr, 'actualValue': value}};
 

instead of the current:

{'pattern': {'requiredPattern': regexStr, 'actualValue': value}};

# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package

@angular/forms

### Description

Angular forms that have controls with multiple `Validator.pattern` validators (which sometimes are very large regex strings) are difficult to map to the correct `<mat-error>` messages.

This can be done by comparing the `requiredPattern` property which is not ideal for large regex strings on large forms. Instead, we are currently forking the `Validator.pattern` code for just to set a different "error" than the default value of "pattern".

### Describe the solution you'd like

Extend the `Validator.pattern` method with an optional parameter that either replaces the `pattern` key or adds a new property inside of the validation error.

Example:

`Validator.pattern( ... , 'my custom error')`

would return an error like:

`{'my custom error': {'requiredPattern': regexStr, 'actualValue': value}};`


or:

`{'pattern': {'error': 'my custom error', 'requiredPattern': regexStr, 'actualValue': value}};`
 

instead of the current:

`{'pattern': {'requiredPattern': regexStr, 'actualValue': value}};`
kept_issues.title: Add option for Validators.pattern to be provided with an custom error to differentiate multiple pattern validators.

# 🚀 Feature Proposal

### Relevant Package
<!-- Can you pin-point one or more @angular/* packages the are relevant for this feature request? -->
<!-- ✍️edit: --> This feature request is for @angular/core


### Description

This proposal adds the first-class support of the [`AbortSignal`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal) web standard.
AbortSignal is not only for Fetch API but will be used for unregistering DOM event listeners. 

[add signal to addEventListener by benjamingr · Pull Request \#919 · whatwg/dom](https://github.com/whatwg/dom/pull/919)

AbortSignal will become a new web-standard for various async tasks. If a component exposes its signal on destroyed, developers can use it for interop to other web-compatible (abortable) APIs.

RxJS team is also considering adding support of AbortSignal for automatic unsubscribing subscriptions.

[Discussion: AbortSignal approach · Issue \#5863 · ReactiveX/rxjs](https://github.com/ReactiveX/rxjs/issues/5863)

### Describe the solution you'd like

This is still a rough idea. I think `ElementRef` can expose its aborting signal.

```ts
@Component()
export class SomeComponent {

  constructor(private elRef: ElementRef) {}

  ngOnInit() {
    const signal: AbortSignal = this.elRef.abortSignal;

    // DOM event
    window.addEventListener('keyup', ..., { signal });

    // Fetch
    fetch(url, {signal}).then(...);

    // RxJS
    someStream$.subscribe(handler, { signal });
  }
}
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered
kept_issues.title: Proposal: Component AbortSignal Support

kept_issues._normalized_body: Currently all async validators in AbstractControl-based classes are merged into a single validator function and subscribe/unsubscribe operation happens for that validator function. This is causing issues when a control has its own async validators + some async validators are added by directives (while constructing a view). When an element which holds a directive is removed from the view (for ex. it has an ngIf on it), we clear the list of validators attached to a control, but if there is a running async validation, it does not get cancelled. There is a PR 40915 that resolves the issue for the cases when only view validators are applied to a control (and there are no other async validators present), but we should rework the subscription mechanisms in AbstractControl class to be more granular to allow cancelling subscription for individual validators. Additional context can be found in PR 40915.

This feature request is for @angular/core


### Description
When we use `@ViewChild`/`ren` or `@ContentChild`/`ren` we can query using DI token and then provide additional `read` option to tell what other token do we want to actually read from it:
```ts
@ViewChild(MyDirective, { read: ElementRef })
readonly element: ElementRef;
```
It would be super awesome if we could do it with constructor params!


### Describe the solution you'd like
Add options to `@Inject` decorator:

```ts
constructor(@Inject(MyContainer, {read: ElementRef}) private readonly myContainerElement: ElementRef) {}
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered
Create tokens and add `useExisting` providers to directives, but it's not always known beforehand what tokens I might need to inject later on.

### Use cases:

1. Querying `ElementRef` of a particular parent element
2. Querying `ChangeDetectorRef` of a wrapping element so content children can trigger change detection of their `OnPush` parent

While doing investigation in a context of 40997, I came across a few areas in Forms module that can be refactored to provide better tree-shaking.

IMPORTANT: I'm creating this ticket primarily to capture some ideas/proposals. The numbers that are used in the ticket are for a particular use-case only, the real result might be different based on a particular scenario.

-------

The use-case that I've looked at was an with an ngModel on it: .

Currently (with Angular 11.2.2) the Forms package size for such use-case is 41.81kb. I've built an app using command from so it's not a fully optimized version (with all optimizations it's 30.11kb). While doing the investigation I prototyped some of the changes to get a sense of potential savings we can get from improved tree-shaking.

1. [PR 41146] Built-in Control Value Accessors are not tree-shakable due to this code:

 

This can be refactored to be tree-shakable by adding a special field onto these classes (for ex ɵbuiltinCVA) and checking if this field exists in the isBuiltInAccessor function instead of referring to these classes directly.

Performing this refactoring allows to drop 10.12kb (~25% reduction), so the Forms package reduced to 31.69kb for that use-case.

2. [PR 41189] Extract some logic from the Validators class and use them directly in the Forms code.

Currently the Validators class contains some helper functions (such as Validators.compose, Validators.composeAsync and Validators.nullValidator) that are used across the code of the Forms package. We should consider extracting these functions, using them directly in the code (to avoid references to Validators class) and use these helpers in the Validators class too (to avoid any breaking changes).

This optimization allows to save 3.36kb (~8% reduction), so the Forms package reduced to 28.33kb for that use-case.

3. Avoid direct references to FormArray and FormGroup in the _find function.

The mentioned _find function is used in the AbstractControl, so once the FormControl is present in the code (which is used under the hood in the NgModel directive), the FormArray and FormGroup become non-tree-shakable as well (even if they are not used anywhere else). Possible refactoring it to do something similar to what I mentioned in the 1st section (regarding Built-in CVAs).

That can give another 7kb of savings (or 16.7% reduction), so the Forms package size is 21.3kb.

4. [PR 41126] I also noticed that the RadioControlRegistry class is non-tree-shakable (as it's directly referenced in the FormsModule and ReactiveFormsModule). We can consider making it a tree-shakable provider (by using providedIn: FormsModule), but that might potentially be a breaking change.

Making RadioControlRegistry tree-shakable saves a bit less than 1kb, so the final Forms package size in my experiment was 20.5kb, which is half the size of the original package (41.81kb).

Note: in real scenarios savings would be much less than in my example, since most of the Forms code would actually be used (such as validators, FormGroup and FormArray, different types of inputs -> more CVAs), but improved tree-shaking should still provide benefits.

We should consider extracting these functions, using them directly in the code (to avoid references to Validators class) and use these helpers in the Validators class too (to avoid any breaking changes).

This optimization allows to save 3.36kb (~8% reduction), so the Forms package reduced to **28.33kb** for that use-case.

3. Avoid direct references to `FormArray` and `FormGroup` in the [_find](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/master/packages/forms/src/model.ts#L48-L71) function.

The mentioned `_find` function is used in the `AbstractControl`, so once the `FormControl` is present in the code (which is used under the hood in the `NgModel` directive), the `FormArray` and `FormGroup` become non-tree-shakable as well (even if they are not used anywhere else). Possible refactoring it to do something similar to what I mentioned in the 1st section (regarding Built-in CVAs).

That can give another 7kb of savings (or 16.7% reduction), so the Forms package size is **21.3kb**.

4. [PR #41126] I also noticed that the `RadioControlRegistry` class is non-tree-shakable (as it's directly referenced in the `FormsModule` and `ReactiveFormsModule`). We can consider making it a tree-shakable provider (by using `providedIn: FormsModule`), but that might potentially be a breaking change.

Making `RadioControlRegistry` tree-shakable saves a bit less than 1kb, so the final Forms package size in my experiment was **20.5kb**, which is half the size of the original package (41.81kb).

Note: in real scenarios savings would be much less than in my example, since most of the Forms code would actually be used (such as validators, FormGroup and FormArray, different types of inputs -> more CVAs), but improved tree-shaking should still provide benefits.
kept_issues.title: Ideas for better tree-shaking of the Forms package

# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package

This feature request is for @angular/core or @angular/compiler (?)

### Description

Angular will currently detect (and complain) if a directive with an input binding exists, but the directive is not known (due to its defining module not being imported):

```
<app-child [myAwesomeDirective]="42"></app-child>
```

However, this doesn't work for directives without an input binding, i.e.

```
<app-child myAwesomeDirective></app-child>
```

The reason for this is – I believe – that `myAwesomeDirective` is treated as an HTML attribute (which makes sense), and HTML attributes are, well, legal HTML. And custom attributes are specifically frequently used as content projection selectors.

However, this causes a couple of issues in the developer experience, specifically

1. No error being shown if you forget to import the module.
2. Making it unsafe to try and identify unused module imports through trial & error of removing them (and there being a lack of alternatives to safely do so).

### Describe the solution you'd like

I don't have a specific solution in mind which I think can be considered good enough. Initially I thought about a new strictness setting which fails on unknown HTML attributes, but especially due to the content projection case this would be problematic and a setting I'd only activate for this specific purpose (which feels awkward); in terms of HTML, there's nothing "illegal" about unknown attributes.

I will point out, however, that IDEs such as IntelliJ can and do warn about unknown HTML attributes, even taking content projection into consideration for this. This is somewhat suitable for case (1), though only for code as you write it, not when e.g. moving a component to a different module, and it doesn't cover (2) which is actually my main concern as there's currently no good way of "housekeeping" module imports in a safe, reliable manner. To clarify, this isn't about tree-shaking, unused modules can of course be tree-shaken, but rather about general maintenance and maybe ultimately even allowing to uninstall unused dependencies.

I'm not sure what, if anything, can be reasonably done here, but would like to at least open this for visibility.

---

To give an example, UI libraries such as Angular Material or ng-zorro-antd require you to import components individually. So you end up importing your buttons, checkboxes, tabs and what have you. But the list only ever grows and can be tough to reduce it down to what is actually needed later on.

<!-- ✍️edit: --> This feature request is for @angular/compiler


### Description
<!-- ✍️-->
The template parser in https://github.com/angular-eslint/angular-eslint works by wrapping the @angular/compiler's `parseTemplate()` and doing some things with the output to teach ESLint what to do with it.

You can use comments in code to tell ESLint when to ignore a section of upcoming code, whether that's the next line, or whole sections delimited by Block comments.

We will be able to offer this same capability in Angular templates (both inline and external HTML files), if the `parseTemplate()` function starts returning an array of comment nodes on the root of the AST that it returns. The root comment nodes array can then be given to ESLint for attachment and everything should work as expected.

Here is example from code and the corresponding comment node structures we would like to emulate:

**source.ts:**
```ts
// a comment
import { foo } from 'bar'
/*
 multiline
*/
```

**Relative bit of AST:**
```jsonc
// ... root of AST
{
  //
  // ... more AST stuff here
  //
  "comments": [
    {
      "type": "Line",
      "value": " a comment",
      "start": 0,
      "end": 12,
      "range": [
        0,
        12
      ],
      "loc": {
        "start": {
          "line": 1,
          "column": 0
        },
        "end": {
          "line": 1,
          "column": 12
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "type": "Block",
      "value": "\n multiline\n",
      "start": 39,
      "end": 55,
      "range": [
        39,
        55
      ],
      "loc": {
        "start": {
          "line": 3,
          "column": 0
        },
        "end": {
          "line": 5,
          "column": 2
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

### Describe the solution you'd like
<!-- ✍️--> If you have a solution in mind, please describe it.

I would like my usage to be something like:

```diff
 const angularCompilerResult = parseTemplate(code, options.filePath, {
    preserveWhitespaces: true,
    preserveLineEndings: true,
+   comments: true
  });
```

And for it to return an array of comment Nodes at the root of the template AST, comparable to the code example above.

This will allow us to close: https://github.com/angular-eslint/angular-eslint/issues/97

### Describe alternatives you've considered
<!-- ✍️--> Have you considered any alternative solutions or workarounds?

We could do an entirely separate parse of the template ourselves using separate tooling I guess, but obviously that would be very wasteful given the @angular/compiler is already doing that and we need the @angular/compiler's AST result anyway.

# 🚀 feature request - parseDate - localizable date parsing, supporting different date formats into date object
### Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/common

### Description
Hello,

on behalf of [Annotation Slovakia s.r.o](https://github.com/AnnotationSro), we would like to propose an extension for date manipulation. 

Throughout multiple projects we have found ourselves dwelling on missing **native** support for date parsing in angular. As a result of this we have been forced to use another "unnecessary" libraries, such as moment.js, or components without ControlValueAccessor, each with custom date parsing implementation.

We have been internally working on [@annotation/ng-datepicker](https://github.com/AnnotationSro/ng-a-datepicker) where we implemented [`parseDate()`](https://github.com/AnnotationSro/ng-a-datepicker/blob/main/ng-a-date-picker/projects/ng-datepicker/src/lib/parsers/parse-date.ts) function, which is based on angular `formatDate()` and we believe it should be part of angular framework. 

We hope you will consider adding this function into framework and as soon as discussion is resolved we will create PR.

Regards.

Martin Filo,
Annotation Slovakia s.r.o.

_Side note:
We are aware of PR #31143, but it was declined as exported utility and it would only work with one date format without localization_

### Demonstartion of `parseDate()` function
**API:**
```
export type BasicDateFormat = 'short' | 'medium' | 'long' | 'full' | 'shortDate' | 'mediumDate' | 'longDate' | 'fullDate' | 'shortTime' | 'mediumTime' | 'longTime' | 'fullTime';
export function parseDate(value: string, format: BasicDateFormat | string, locale: string, oldValue?: Date): Date;
```

**Example usage 1:** 
```
const dateString: string = '2021-01-27T22:37:44+02:00';
const format: string = 'yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ssZZZZZ';

const date: Date = parseDate(dateString, format, 'sk', undefined);
// date = Wed Jan 27 2021 21:37:44 GMT+0100 (Central European Standard Time)
```

**Example usage 2:** 
```
const dateString: string = '1.1.2020';
const format: BasicDateFormat = 'shortDate';

const date: Date = parseDate(dateString, format, 'sk', undefined);
// date = Wed Jan 01 2020 01:00:00 GMT+0100 (Central European Standard Time)
```

### Describe the solution you'd like
We would like to open a discussion about this feature and as soon as it is approved we will create PR

# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package

@angular/compiler

### Description
Ivy compiler requires all `@Component` metadata to be resolved statically. So generally it's not possible to declare an array of styles of style URLs in a different buildable units and use them in the current one, since the actual values would not be available in D.TS files (only corresponding type declarations). However declaring such arrays with `as const` modifier pulls the value into D.TS files and Ivy compiler can technically leverage this information:

In TS:
```
const styles = ['margin: 0px', 'padding: 0px'] as const;
const styleUrls = ['./style-a.css', './style-b.css'] as const;
```

Corresponding D.TS:
```
declare const styles: readonly ["margin: 0px", "padding: 0px"];
declare const styleUrls: readonly ["./style-a.css", "./style-b.css"];
```

(same example in [TypeScript playground](https://www.typescriptlang.org/play?ssl=3&ssc=63&pln=2&pc=1#code/MYewdgzgLgBFCmBbADgGwIYJgXhgcnQCNg8BuAKFElmgE9V4IcYBtPRdAJwHMBLMAFwwADMgAeeADT5k6ACZz+3IaIkBdGOiZVoFHTSj14AVU6omuNgDoA9HQYBadFeAQIU-LfvwHhF27wNLRh9CiA))

Currently the compiler's static evaluation can understand string literal types, but not tuple types.
kept_issues.title: Consider supporting `styles` and `styleUrls` defined with `as const` in different buildable units

Right now, the cleanupCaches() function from the service-worker implementation evicts versions of the application that are not present in the Clients list.

However, as stated in the comment for this function:

> This may skip some clients in the browser back-forward cache, but not much can be done about that.

I thought, that we could use a reasonable TTL to make the cache eviction a little bit safer. Namely:

In other words: the application could be removed from the cache when the assigned client ID is no longer present and after the specific time has passed since the last use of this version.

This will ensure that even if a browser has cached some version of the application in it's back-forward cache it can still be used (during the specified TTL period).

I'm willing to implement this feature if it will be considered useful.

Don't know about any alternative solutions.

### Relevant Package
This feature request is for `@angular/service-worker`.

### Description
Right now, the [cleanupCaches()](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/3a823abcc554cffdda1e14e181dadad9063701de/packages/service-worker/worker/src/driver.ts#L890) function from the service-worker implementation evicts versions of the application that are not present in the [Clients](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Clients) list.

However, as stated in the comment for this function:

> This may skip some clients in the browser back-forward cache, but not much can be done about that.

### Describe the solution you'd like
I thought, that we could use a reasonable TTL to make the cache eviction a little bit safer. Namely:

1. we assign a `last access time` property to each version of the application and update it each time when the specific version is used by the client.
2. we configure a reasonable TTL value, e.g. 24 hours
3. during the cache cleanup we add an additional step to determine if the version could be safely evicted from the cache by comparing `last access time` for this version with the TTL.

In other words: the application could be removed from the cache when the assigned client ID is no longer present and after the specific time has passed since the last use of this version.

This will ensure that even if a browser has cached some version of the application in it's back-forward cache it can still be used (during the specified TTL period).

I'm willing to implement this feature if it will be considered useful.

### Describe alternatives you've considered
Don't know about any alternative solutions.
kept_issues.title: proposal: use TTL and last access time to evict unused versions from service-worker's cache

🚀 feature request

 Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/packages/router and @angular/angular.

 Description
In order to increase accessibility and build in best practices, allow an option to provide a unique page title to each path in the Angular router. 

 TitleService vs Proposed Change
Currently the TitleService allows us to manage page title, which allows developers to add unique page titles. This requires additional work for developers and the contextual knowledge to understand that this not only a best practice, but that page title _needs_ to be managed in order to make your application more accessible. 

Eventually I'd like to see this option enforced as mandatory or throw a warning if not defined, to ensure Angular apps are more accessible by default. This known property could also be more easily caught with a lint rule.

 Context
W3 defines that page title must be unique. Angular is a single-page app and, as a result, a majority of transitions, such as moving to a new page, do not involve a page reload. This means that out of the box, each page is read with an identical page title, and provides no value for understanding the page's content or purpose for users using a11y services.

 Proposed feature
Define a know title property in the router's route definitions, which is then subscribed to automatically and uses the TitleService under the hood to manage page title on routing automatically.

 

 Describe alternatives you've considered
TitleService works, but again, it puts the burden on the developer to know about this single page app accessibility pitfall and how to implement unique page titles (and manage subscribing to the router ActivatedRoute or manage title in each route's component).

# 🚀 feature request

### Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/packages/router and @angular/angular.


### Description
In order to increase accessibility and build in best practices, allow an option to provide a unique page title to each path in the Angular router. 


#### TitleService vs Proposed Change
Currently the TitleService allows us to manage page title, which allows developers to add unique page titles. This requires additional work for developers and the contextual knowledge to understand that this not only a best practice, but that page title _needs_ to be managed in order to make your application more accessible. 

Eventually I'd like to see this option enforced as mandatory or throw a warning if not defined, to ensure Angular apps are more accessible by default. This known property could also be more easily caught with a lint rule.

#### Context
W3 defines that [page title must be unique](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/page-titled). Angular is a single-page app and, as a result, a majority of transitions, such as moving to a new page, do not involve a page reload. This means that out of the box, each page is read with an identical page title, and provides no value for understanding the page's content or purpose for users using a11y services.


### Proposed feature
Define a know `title` property in the router's route definitions, which is then subscribed to automatically and uses the TitleService under the hood to manage page title on routing automatically.

```ts
const routes: Routes = [
  { path: 'chicken', component: ChickenComponent, title: 'Chicken - Farm Demo App' },
  { path: 'goat', component: GoatComponent, title: 'Goat - Farm Demo App' },
  { path: 'frog', component: FrogComponent, title: 'Frog - Farm Demo App' },
  { path: '',   redirectTo: '/goat', pathMatch: 'full' }, // redirects ok without a title
  { path: '**', component: HomeComponent }, // throws warning with no title prop defined
];
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered
TitleService works, but again, it puts the burden on the developer to know about this single page app accessibility pitfall and how to implement unique page titles (and manage subscribing to the router ActivatedRoute or manage title in each route's component).
kept_issues.title: Define unique page titles in the Angular router (a11y)

🚀 Feature request

 Relevant Package
This feature request is for @angular/common in particular for the DatePipe.

 Description
The available pre-defined formats for DatePipe as per [documentation] supports textual formats (i.e. "June 15, 2015" or "9:03 AM") that show month names or AM/PM times.

For some applications it would be useful to support long numerical formats (i.e. "6/15/2015 09:03.00") and take into account the locale to switch day and month in english and non-english format.

[documentation]: 

 Describe the solution you'd like
I would suggest adding these pre-defined formats:
- "numerical" = "MM/dd/yyyy HH:mm:ss" (english) and "dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm:ss" (non-english)
- "numericalDate" = "MM/dd/yyyy" (english) and "dd/MM/yyyy" (non-english)
- "numericalTime" = "HH:mm:ss" (both english and non-english)

 Describe alternatives you've considered
At this moment the only supported option is using a custom format and manually take into account the locale, which requires extra effort and is error-prone.

Feature Request

When porting my library to v12 I've tried compiling with the partial-ivy recommended mode.
This resulted in a never ending bombardment of NG3003 errors due to cyclic dependencies. 

The current library compilation is very strict which results in

- Poor library developer experience
- Workaround manoeuvres to make it compile resulting in less code readability which makes it more difficult for devs to enter into open source projects.

First, i'll say that such a breaking change, from warning to error should have been introduces gradually. 
These are not pure cyclic dependencies, they don't result in a null reference since the symbols are used later.

I understand that it compromises efficient tree shaking. 
Ok, for hard-references throw the error, but why does it also throw for soft-references, symbols used only for type annotation on properties etc... those that are not Input, Output, DI... it will throw for those soft references as well.

What's more confusing is that type imports is also not supported...
Even with import type { X } from './y' it will complain about X being a cyclic dependency.

I almost ran out of trick until I found something which works:

 

And now I can use that type without issues.

This limitation should improve as it forces the developer to write funky code which he wouldn't write otherwise.
The docs recommend bad practices to workaround this as well.

I understand the reason behind forcing authors to build efficient tree-shakable libraries, although allowing to control the volume of this restriction would be nice.

Moreover, soft-references and surely type imports are not cyclic by all means and are not used for metadata by angular so they should not throw.

I'm now required to refactor a 4 year old repo with lot's of code, frustrating.

Thanks :)

# Feature Request

When porting my library to v12 I've tried compiling with the **partial-ivy** recommended mode.
This resulted in a never ending bombardment of **NG3003** errors due to cyclic dependencies.  

The current library compilation is very strict which results in

- Poor library developer experience
-  Workaround manoeuvres to make it compile resulting in less code readability which makes it more difficult for devs to enter into open source projects.

First, i'll say that such a breaking change, from warning to error should have been introduces gradually.  
These are not pure cyclic dependencies, they don't result in a null reference since the symbols are used later.

I understand that it compromises efficient tree shaking. 
Ok, for hard-references throw the error, but why does it also throw for soft-references, symbols used only for type annotation on properties etc... those that **are not** Input, Output, DI... it will throw for those soft references as well.

What's more confusing is that type imports is also not supported...
Even with  `import type { X } from './y'` it will complain about `X` being a cyclic dependency.

I almost ran out of trick until I found something which works:

```ts
// tokens.ts
export type X = import('./y').X;
```

And now I can use that type without issues.

This limitation should improve as it forces the developer to write funky code which he wouldn't write otherwise.
The docs recommend bad practices to workaround this as well.

I understand the reason behind forcing authors to build efficient tree-shakable libraries, although allowing to control the volume of this restriction would be nice.

Moreover, soft-references and surely type imports are not cyclic by all means and are not used for metadata by angular so they should not throw.

I'm now required to refactor a 4 year old repo with lot's of code, frustrating.

Thanks :)
kept_issues.title: Improve library compiler cyclic dependency detector (NG3003)

# Feature Request ### Relevant Package @angular/localize Previous issue about this feature: https://github.com/angular/angular/issues/35912 (auto closed) ### Description With the new `$localize` in Ivy we are finally able to do translations in code. This allows us to have strings in services or components (.ts files - "code") that are translated, which allows for very nice APIs. For example we can now open a modal or toast from an error handler somewhere inside of a service without creating a new component for every error message. Tagging strings in components is very similar to using templates: ```
Submit
``` ```const buttonLabel = ':@@myId.buttonLabeal:Submit';``` However there is a difference in functionality. **In code, you cannot use plurals or other ICU messages**. For example, we have a pipe like this since our api returns numbers as `{ value: number, unit: string }`: ```ts const value: number = input.value; const transformedValue = this.decimalPipe.transform(value, '1.0-2'); const unitMessages = { gal: $localize`:@@units.gal.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 gallon} other {${transformedValue} gallons}}`, gallons: $localize`:@@units.gallons.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 gallon} other {${transformedValue} gallons}}`, hl: $localize`:@@units.hl.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 hectoliter} other {${transformedValue} hectoliters}}`, liters: $localize`:@@units.liters.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 liter} other {${transformedValue} liters}}`, litres: $localize`:@@units.litres.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 liter} other {${transformedValue} liters}}`, pg: $localize`:@@units.pg.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 proof gallon} other {${transformedValue} proof gallons}}`, kg: $localize`:@@units.kg.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 kilogram} other {${transformedValue} kilograms}}`, lbs: $localize`:@@units.lbs.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 pound} other {${transformedValue} pounds}}`, tonne: $localize`:@@units.tonne.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 tonne} other {${transformedValue} tonnes}}`, tons: $localize`:@@units.tons.long:{${value}, plural, =1 {1 ton} other {${transformedValue} tons}}`, } return unitMessages[input.unit]: // Will return a translated ICU message - without replacing the plural ``` This is because in templates the compiler actually rewrites ICU pluralMessages into an ngSwitch. This also has the drawback that it only supports a subset of what is supported in ICU (see https://github.com/angular/angular/issues/9117) ### Describe the solution you'd like It would be great to have feature parity between code i18n and template i18n. It could make sense to have a separate ICU message parser / compiler that does not generate an angular template AST but a JS AST instead. That way we could use the same implementation both from code and template. For example js-lingui does it this way - messages are parsed during build time and compiled into functions. E.g. ```{value, plural, = 1 {1 gallon} other {# gallons}``` gets compiled to something like ```const t1 = value => value === 1 ? "1 gallon" : value + " gallons";```. There are libraries that use this concept, for example lingui or @messageformat/compiler. Alternatively the message could be parsed and interpreted at runtime. ### Describe alternatives you've considered To solve this without a change to angular it would be possible to expose a global function and ship a library like @messageformat/core to parse & execute the translated ICU messages returned by $localize. This would increase bundle size a lot. Another alternative would be to stick to template translations. This requires the kind of ugly workaround that are luckily no longer needed for strings without plurals - thanks to the fantastic `@angular/localize` package!
kept_issues.title: Support ICU messages (e.g. Plurals) at runtime $localize and create feature parity with template i18n

I use Angular for years with complex applications, and i've still troubles with performance on big page with many components !
I'm aware with usual tricks (ChangeDetector, trackBy, mutability, etc..), but it's not enough. To my mind, it's the limit of Angular and i'm asking to myself to better use VueJS or React (what a shame).

I think that actual Change Detection Strategies are not enough and we should go further.
I think that global strategy is good, but we should be able to be more specific on wich property should be watched (and maybe set a different strategy for each property should be better). Because on complex object, we need to use properties for private and local use only, and there is no needto watch them).

My proposal : 
- Introduce ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnWatch : when set, we need to set manually if a property must be watched or not (by default, same behavior as default, but do not watch all properties of the components to detect changes).
- Add new Watch() annotation which can be used on class properties. For complex object, maybe a 'deep' attribute can be used to define if only the ref should be watched, or all the properties of the object property).

This way is similar to OnPush Strategy / @Input() annotation, but introduce more flexibility (to my mind), and prevent Angular to trigger detect changes for everything if not needed.

Feature Request

 Relevant Package

@angular/compiler and @angular/compiler-cli

 Description

Introduce compile-time conformance checks to guard against performance anti-patterns.

 Describe the solution you'd like

The Angular compiler can perform extra checks on the user application to guard against common pitfalls. We already have the available parsing and reporting infrastructure, and there's work happening in the direction of expanding the number of compile-time checks.

A few examples of helpful performance conformance rules are:

- Find all the unused components, directives, and pipes in the hierarchy of @NgModule and report them.
- Inline styles within component templates. They are going to break CSS inlining and also view encapsulation.
- Prevent adding fonts within component template. Rather, prefer adding fonts globally to index.html.
- Check if there's a relative anchor without a routerLink attribute. This is often a user mistake that can cause the page to reload rather than trigger a client-side navigation

 Describe alternatives you've considered

An alternative is to delegate these checks to linters, such as eslint or codelyzer (now deprecated). Even though this would reduce maintenance, we'd also be limited to only applications using the linting tooling and have explicitly enabled these checks.
