 Description

The afterRender and afterNextRender hooks currently trigger on _any_ change detection. This could include a call to ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges. There is no way to create a render hook that only runs when the global change detection is triggered (i.e. ApplicationRef.tick). 

This is especially problematic for afterNextRender when the intent is almost always to run after the next global change detection or "after rendering _this_ component". The problem is that there might be a ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges call before the global ApplicationRef.tick might happen. This would mean that the component may not have been change detected/rendered when the hook runs.

 Proposed solution

Add a property to the AfterRenderOptions to only run the hook after a _global_ change detection (ApplicationRef.tick) rather than running it on _any_ change detection (ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges).

 Alternatives considered

There's no alternative at the moment.

providers: [

providers: [

 Description

The goal of the feature request should be to describe a behavior that was (partially) possible with NgModules.

For this proposal the word “bundle” will be used to describe a concept, of components, directives, pipes and/ or services combined in one unit. This is not not meant as a goal, but as a semantic/ technical detail to talk about in this proposal.

As a developer in a large Angular code base I want to combine components, directives, pipes, and services to a bundle (in the past NgModule). 
The goal should be to enforce some form of boundaries, to avoid duplicate imports of components and define an API for a bundle in the form of components, directives, pipes and services that can be accessed from other parts of the application. With this concept we can logically isolate parts of the application (e.g. for lazy features) and import a bundle of components.
The boundaries would prevent code quality problems like spaghetti code, especially in larger teams/ projects. Developers define the intended use of larger chunks of components, directives, pipes and services by making clear what is exposed.

 NgModules solved this problem partially.

As we want to avoid NgModules in favor of Standalone Components in the future, we need to find a different alternative, that is not adding the same overhead of NgModules in a different way.

 Proposed solution

This is open for discussion, as a solution is not obvious yet

 Alternatives considered

An alternative to enforce the boundary problem is currently possible is to use Nx’s Standalone Application setup, which allows one application to have multiple libraries and define the API interface of those libraries by defining an index.ts file for each library. This is supported by the @nx/enforce-module-boundaries eslint rule, which allows other libraries and the application to only import components, directives, pipes, and services that are defined in the index.ts file. This way we can define and enforce a clear API for other developers for a semantically connected bundle of components, directives, pipes, and services, without actually defining, developing, and deploying separate libraries.

### Which @angular/* package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request?

service-worker

### Description

Currently you can use Push notification for displaying notification messages. But it is not possible to change application badge from push notification when application is not started. 
You can use setAppBadge from SwPush.messages, but this only works when application is already running. 


### Proposed solution

Support setting application badge natively in ngsw-worker.js. New push payload would look something like this:
```typescript
{
  "notification": {
    "actions": NotificationAction[],
    ....
  },
  "appBadge": number | undefined
}
```
If appBadge property is not set nothing will happened, but if it is set, then inside "push" event, self.navigator.setAppBadge should be called with value of "appBadge". Setting "appBadge" to 0, will clear badge.


### Alternatives considered

Now the only way to change application badge when application is offline is to use custom service worker to handle "push" event and then import ngsw-worker.js. But I'm not sure that even this will work on WebKit, because as stated in https://webkit.org/blog/14112/badging-for-home-screen-web-apps/ and if I understand correctly, both showNotification and setAppBadge must be 'promise' from same "push" event.

 Description

For typical CRUD operations, it's often required to
- reset the dialog to its initial state
- query if a particular FormControl has a value that's different than the original one.

Problem :

 Proposed solution

Proposal :

HTML
 
Benefits :

1. Optimized initial load: Load only the essential code for the user's device, reducing initial bundle size and improving load time.

 Description

In Angular, the reusability of components is a core feature but leads to potential conflicts with HTML standards regarding the uniqueness of id attributes within a document. It particularly impacts accessibility (with aria-labelledby attributes expecting unique id values) and form handling (where label elements use the for attribute to reference input elements by id). 

 Proposed solution

Introduce a new field in the component decorator to enable automatic ID uniqueness on a per-instance basis. When this boolean field is set to true, would instruct Angular to automatically prefix id, for, aria-labelledby, and any other attributes that reference IDs, with a unique component instance identifier, ensuring that every instance of a component has uniquely identifiable elements without additional effort from developers.

 Alternatives considered

1. Currently, developers can manually manage unique IDs by incrementing an identifier for each component instance. This approach is simple but prone to human error.
 
2. Another workaround involves creating custom directives (e.g., [uid] and [ufor]) that communicate through a service to ensure ID uniqueness within the same component instance. Due to the lack of direct references to component instances, this method requires implementing a custom mechanism to track and associate directive instances with their respective component instances. This adds a layer of complexity, as developers must ensure accurate tracking and synchronization across component lifecycles, making it a less than ideal solution.
kept_issues.title: Unique ID generation for component instances

kept_issues.body:
### Which @angular/* package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request?

core

### Description

Currently, `toSignal` and `toObservable` functions always return read-only primitives - `Signal` and `Observable` respectively. It would be really handy if passing a writable primitive to interop functions created a writable counterpart of passed value.

Examples:

```ts
const someSignal = signal(1)
effect(() => {
  const value = someSignal()
  console.log('signal changed:', value)
})

const someSubject = toObservable() // returned a Subject!
someSubject.next(2) // signal changed: 2
```

```ts
const someSubject = new Subject(1)
someSubject.subscribe(value => console.log('subject changed:', value)

const someSignal = toSignal(someSubject) // returned a WritableSignal!
someSignal.set(2) // => subject changed: 2
someSignal.update(prev => prev * 2) // => subject changed: 4
```

### Proposed solution

Return a `WritableSignal` from `toSignal` if argument is `next`-able. Whenever a value is written to the signal manually, push it to the target observable.

In `toObservable`, return a subject if argument is a `WritableSignal`. Whenever a value is pushed to the subject manually, write it to the target signal.

### Alternatives considered

Leave everything as is.
kept_issues.title: rxjs-interop: bidirectional interop

### Which @angular/* package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request?

core

### Description

Suppose I have some state `imageBlob: Signal<Blob>` and I want some derived state `imageBlobUrl: Signal<string>` using `URL.createBlobURL` (perhaps so I can display it in an `img` element). Naively, I could define `imageBlobUrl` as:
```typescript
imageBlobUrl = computed(() => URL.createBlobURL(imageBlob()))
```
However, this would leak the object URLs. Where should I call `URL.revokeObjectURL`?

*(`URL.createBlobURL`/`URL.revokeObjectURL` could, of course, be substituted for any resource that needs explicit cleanup, like an open `WritableStream`, an open WebSocket, a handle into WASM memory, etc.)*

### Proposed solution

`computed` could take an additional option `cleanup` that is called some (unspecified) time after a `computed`'s value changes with the previous value:
```typescript
imageBlobUrl = computed(() => URL.createBlobURL(imageBlob()), {cleanup: URL.revokeObjectURL})
```

Alternatively, `computed` could adopt an API similar to `effect` for registering a cleanup callback (though for this particular example it's much more cumbersome):
```typescript
imageBlobUrl = computed((onCleanup) => {
  const ret = URL.createBlobURL(imageBlob());
  onCleanup(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(ret));
  return ret;
})
```

Note that these APIs avoid introducing statefulness/hysteresis into `computed` and don't specify the exact timing of when the cleanup function will be called (sidestepping https://github.com/angular/angular/issues/56186#issuecomment-2173063032).

A similar API could be adopted for `signal` too, though, since changes are fully user-controlled, it's easy make a wrapper that does the cleanup immediately before calling `set`.

### Alternatives considered

- document workarounds:
  - Angular documentation should commit to the position that situations like this *require* piping though RxJS or an `effect` with `allowSignalWrites`
  - Angular documentation should point users to the "hack" of saving the previous value in a closure (or to a nicely-packaged version of that hack, e.g. ngxtension's [`extendedComputed`](https://ngxtension.netlify.app/utilities/signals/computed/) or [`computedPrevious`](https://ngxtension.netlify.app/utilities/signals/computed-previous/))

### See also:
- #56186
- #54339

A flag system would empower me to explicitly opt out of these features and ensure my code remains maintainable and future-proof, allowing me to continue using established syntaxes while still having the option to adopt newer ones as I see fit.

All current deprications will be removed

One might also then be able to opt in for a set of specific new language features
As this lives at the project level special attention should be put to imports, as external imports may involve different flag setups.

 Alternatives considered

Freeze the language, no more deprecations, but add extension modules to enrich the language.

### Description

If I want to pass signal based data to a `ComponentRef` we have to set the input and create an effect to update the input.

```ts
const counterSignal = signal<number>(0) // signal from store or some service

const counterOverlayRef = createOverlay(); // using CDK Overlay
```

```ts
const counterSignal = signal<number>(0) // signal from store or some service
```

### Which @angular/* package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request?

_No response_

### Description


### Problem
Angular Router currently supports `**` only as a catch-all at the end of a route. It lacks support for multi-segment wildcards *between* fixed segments—e.g., `/foo/**/bar` should match `/foo/a/bar`, `/foo/a/b/c/bar`, but not `/foo/bar`.

The only workaround today is a custom `UrlMatcher`, which introduces unnecessary complexity, boilerplate, and testing burden for a common pattern.

### Proposal

### Component Access
Intermediate segments could be exposed via `ActivatedRoute`, e.g.:

```ts
const segments = route.snapshot.paramMap.get('wildcardSegments');
```
Allow `**` to be used between segments in the `path` property:

```ts
{ path: 'foo/**/bar', component: MyComponent }
```

Matching rules:
- Must start with `foo`, end with `bar`
- Must include one or more intermediate segments

### Which @angular/* package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request?

`@angular/core` (and `@angular/compiler`?)

### Description

Currently, when using custom elements (e.g., Web Components) within an Angular application, developers must declare CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA either at the module level (e.g., NgModule.schemas) or component level (@Component.schemas). This global declaration effectively tells the Angular compiler to ignore any unknown elements within the entire scope, which can lead to a less strict template validation than desired, as it disables validation for all unknown elements, even those not intended to be custom elements.

It is of course possible to create small components that have the CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA. However, it is more difficult to maintain the quality of those templates over time. A pull request with only a HTML change would not show the schema that applies.

This proposal aims to introduce a mechanism to apply the CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA only to a specific, localized scope within an Angular template, leveraging the new @-prefixed control flow syntax. This would allow developers to precisely define where custom elements are expected, thus maintaining stricter template validation for the rest of the template and improving developer experience by reducing unnecessary global declarations.

### Proposed solution

I would like to propose a syntax to allow custom elements within a defined scope of a component template.

The syntax would look like this:
```HTML
@schema(CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA) {
<fluent-card class="custom">
    <fluent-progress value="64"></fluent-progress>
    @schema(ANGULAR_DEFAULT_SCHEMA) {
        <app-example>This component should still exist</app-example>
    }
</fluent-card>
}
```
This way, you can define blocks within a template where a schema applies. In this proposal ANGULAR_DEFAULT_SCHEMA would refer to the schema that Angular applies by default if no other schema is defined. The example shows how you can nest this syntax to apply different schema's to nested HTML in the template.

The schema should be provided as a value.

By defining the schema within the template, it's less likely that the applied schema is overlooked, and it introduces enough flexibility to still apply validation where that is desired.

### Alternatives considered

Having block scopes makes the template more verbose. I did consider having element scoped schema's, for example:
```HTML
<fluent-card class="custom" @schema="CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA">
    <fluent-progress value="64" @schema="CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA" />
    <app-example>This component should still exist</app-example>
</fluent-card>
```

But having the block scope notation leaves no questions about the scope of the schema.

Alternatively I did consider a notation like the one below, but I feel it's just difficult to read (and the element name could become a variable, with potential complex results):

```HTML
<ng-element ngElementName="fluent-card" class="custom">
    <app-example>This component still exists</app-example>
</ng-element>
```

Optionally it could be nice to also have this feature as a structural directive (*ngSchema="CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA"), similar to how `@if` has an *ngIf alternative. But since there is no *ngLet, I considered to leave this scenario out of the proposal.

---

Alternatively a more adaptable schema could be considered:
```
schemas: [REGEX_SCHEMA(/^fluent\-/i)]
```
However, this could lead to complex regular expressions or a regex that could degrade performance.

---

It is of course possible to create small components that have the CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA. However, it is more difficult to maintain the quality of those templates over time. A pull request with only a HTML change would not show the schema that applies, leading the reviewer to assume that the used element names are correct.
kept_issues.title: Narrow the scope of the CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA schema

 Description

Suggesting a new compiler mode that compiles most Angular template logic directly into vanilla JavaScript/DOM operations, leaving only a small runtime kernel for dependency injection and reactive signals. This could dramatically reduce bundle size and improve startup performance, especially for mobile and embedded applications.

Motivation:
Angular’s Ivy compiler already emits fine-grained JS instructions.
With the recent move to Signals and away from Zone.js, Angular could further minimize its runtime dependency.
Similar “compile away the framework” approaches (e.g., Svelte, Solid) show strong performance benefits.

Benefits:
- Reduced bundle size and faster cold starts
- Lower memory usage
- Potential “Angular Lite” variant for low-resource environments

Related Work:
- React Compiler (Forget)
- Svelte compile-to-DOM approach
- Angular Ivy / Signals architecture

 Proposed solution

Extend AOT to inline static template bindings as direct DOM operations.
Retain a minimal runtime for DI, event binding, and reactive state updates.
Make this an opt-in build mode to preserve backward compatibility.

 Alternatives considered

Relying on Ivy AOT compilation alone: Angular’s Ahead-of-Time compilation and tree-shaking already reduce runtime overhead, but they still depend on a fairly large core runtime (zone.js, change detection, DI). This proposal goes further by removing most of that runtime for static components.

 Description

When submitting an invalid form, focusing the first invalid field is an important accessibility practice (WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification). However, the current API only allows focusing based on data model order, not template order.

Currently, errorSummary().at(0) returns the first invalid field based on the order of properties in the form data model, not the order they appear in the template. This leads to unexpected focus behavior and poor user experience, especially for screen reader users who expect focus to move to the first error in reading order.

Reproduction:

 

Expected behavior: The title field should be focused (first in template).

Actual behavior: The ISBN field is focused (first in data model).

Workaround: Reordering properties in the data model to match template order, but this is not maintainable and couples data structure to UI concerns.

Maybe there is a simple solution already available which I havent discovered yet.

 Proposed solution

A high level API to set the focus to first invalid field based on DOM/template order:

 

Or a method to get the first invalid field based on DOM/template order:

 

 Alternatives considered

Manual DOM traversal: Query all invalid fields via querySelectorAll('[aria-invalid="true"]') and focus the first one. This works but bypasses the Signal Forms API entirely and feels like a workaround.

Reorder data model: Change property order in the data model to match template order. This is not maintainable and creates tight coupling between data structure and UI.

Custom sorting: Manually sort errorSummary() results by DOM position before focusing. This is verbose and requires boilerplate code in every form submission handler.

Which @angular/ package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request?

compiler

 Description

When @deprecated symbols are used in Angular templates, there is currently no compiler diagnostic emitted during build. This includes:

- Inputs, outputs, and models of components/directives marked @deprecated (via JSDoc)
- Public/protected properties and methods accessed in template expressions when marked @deprecated
- Components/directives/pipes used in the template when the class itself is @deprecated _(partially detectable today — see below)_

 What is currently detectable

Deprecated components, directives, and pipes can be partially detected today via @typescript-eslint/no-deprecated on the .ts file, because they appear in the imports array of the consuming component (only works for standalone use):

 

However, this only tells you that the import exists — it does not tell you _where_ in the template the deprecated selector is used, nor does it help when a non-deprecated component exposes deprecated members.

 What is NOT detectable today

There is no way to detect the following during build or in CI:

1. Deprecated inputs/outputs/models:

 

 

2. Deprecated public properties/methods in template expressions:

 

 

The Angular Language Service in VS Code correctly detects all of the above and shows deprecated symbols as ~~strikethrough~~, but this information is not available during compilation (ng build / ngc), meaning deprecated usages in templates cannot be caught in CI pipelines.

 Why this cannot be fully solved with a lint rule

This problem cannot be fully addressed by any existing or custom ESLint rule, because it requires resolving type information across the boundary between TypeScript and HTML templates:

- @typescript-eslint/no-deprecated operates on .ts files only. It can catch deprecated components/directives/pipes at the import site (in the imports array), but it has no visibility into external .html template files. It cannot detect deprecated inputs/outputs/models, deprecated property/method access in template expressions, or pinpoint where a deprecated selector is used in the template.
- @angular-eslint/template-parser parse the template AST, but this AST only contains structural information (element names, attribute names, expressions). It does not resolve which component class a given element maps to, nor does it have access to the TypeScript type metadata of that component's inputs/outputs. Therefore, a template lint rule has no way to know whether [icon] refers to a deprecated input().
- The only layer that has both the template AST and the full TypeScript type information is the Angular compiler itself. This is why an extended diagnostic is the appropriate solution — the compiler already performs template type-checking and has all the information needed to emit this warning.

 Justification

This diagnostic fits the extended diagnostics criteria:

- Common, non-obvious mistake: Developers have no way to know a template binding or expression targets a deprecated symbol unless they hover over it in VS Code. This is especially problematic for inputs/outputs/models, which are completely invisible to existing lint tools.
- The why is clear: Deprecated symbols are typically removed in future versions, causing runtime breakage. Detecting them early reduces migration costs.
- Clear solution: The diagnostic message includes the replacement from the @deprecated JSDoc.
- Low false-positive rate: If a symbol is marked @deprecated, any usage is a true positive.
- Applies to all Angular applications: Any project consuming libraries or shared components with deprecated members benefits.
- Improves program correctness: Prevents future breakage during library/component upgrades.

 Proposed solution

Add a new extended diagnostic (e.g. deprecatedSymbolInTemplate) that emits a warning when a template references any @deprecated symbol.

The diagnostic should detect:

- Bindings to @deprecated inputs: [inputName]="expr", inputName="value" (both signal input() and legacy @Input() decorator)
- Bindings to @deprecated outputs: (outputName)="handler()" (both output() and legacy @Output() decorator)
- Bindings to @deprecated models: [(modelName)]="expr" (two-way binding via model())
- Usage of @deprecated components/directives via their selector: , [deprecatedDirective]
- Usage of @deprecated pipes in expressions: {{ value | deprecatedPipe }}
- Access to @deprecated public properties/methods in template expressions: {{ obj.deprecatedProp }}, (click)="deprecatedMethod()"
- Include the deprecation message from the JSDoc tag in the diagnostic message, so developers know the recommended replacement
- Be configurable as warning (default), error, or suppress via angularCompilerOptions.extendedDiagnostics, like all other extended diagnostics

Example diagnostic outputs:

 

 Alternatives considered

Angular Language Service: Detects all cases in the IDE (shows deprecated symbols as ~~strikethrough~~), but is not usable in CI. A possible alternative would be for the Language Service to expose a CLI or a --diagnostics mode that could report deprecated usages across a project, similar to how tsc --noEmit reports type errors. However, this would essentially duplicate the work of extended diagnostics, and integrating the check directly into the compiler keeps the toolchain simpler.

### Which @angular/* package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request?

compiler

### Description

When `@deprecated` symbols are used in Angular templates, there is currently **no compiler diagnostic** emitted during build. This includes:

- **Inputs, outputs, and models** of components/directives marked `@deprecated` (via JSDoc)
- **Public/protected properties and methods** accessed in template expressions when marked `@deprecated`
- **Components/directives/pipes** used in the template when the class itself is `@deprecated` _(partially detectable today — see below)_

### What is currently detectable

Deprecated **components**, **directives**, and **pipes** can be partially detected today via `@typescript-eslint/no-deprecated` on the `.ts` file, because they appear in the `imports` array of the consuming component (only works for standalone use):

```typescript
@Component({
  imports: [
    DeprecatedComponent, // ← @typescript-eslint/no-deprecated catches this
  ],
})
export class ParentComponent {}
```

However, this only tells you that the import exists — it does **not** tell you _where_ in the template the deprecated selector is used, nor does it help when a non-deprecated component exposes deprecated members.

#### What is NOT detectable today

There is **no way** to detect the following during build or in CI:

**1. Deprecated inputs/outputs/models:**

```typescript
@Component({
  selector: 'my-component',
  template: '...',
})
export class MyComponent {
  /** @deprecated Use `iconUrl` instead. */
  readonly icon = input<string>();

  readonly iconUrl = input<string>();
}
```

```html
<!-- No warning emitted -->
<my-component [icon]="'some-icon'" />
```

**2. Deprecated public properties/methods in template expressions:**

```typescript
export class MyComponent {
  /** @deprecated Use `newItems()` instead. */
  readonly items = computed(() => []);

  readonly newItems = computed(() => []);
}
```

```html
<!-- No warning emitted -->
@for (item of items(); track item.id) { ... }
```

The **Angular Language Service** in VS Code correctly detects all of the above and shows deprecated symbols as ~~strikethrough~~, but this information is **not available during compilation** (`ng build` / `ngc`), meaning deprecated usages in templates cannot be caught in CI pipelines.

### Why this cannot be fully solved with a lint rule

This problem **cannot be fully addressed by any existing or custom ESLint rule**, because it requires resolving type information across the boundary between TypeScript and HTML templates:

- **`@typescript-eslint/no-deprecated`** operates on `.ts` files only. It can catch deprecated components/directives/pipes **at the import site** (in the `imports` array), but it has no visibility into external `.html` template files. It cannot detect deprecated inputs/outputs/models, deprecated property/method access in template expressions, or pinpoint where a deprecated selector is used in the template.
- **`@angular-eslint/template-parser`** parse the template AST, but this AST only contains structural information (element names, attribute names, expressions). It does **not** resolve which component class a given element maps to, nor does it have access to the TypeScript type metadata of that component's inputs/outputs. Therefore, a template lint rule has no way to know whether `[icon]` refers to a deprecated `input()`.
- The **only layer that has both** the template AST and the full TypeScript type information is the **Angular compiler** itself. This is why an extended diagnostic is the appropriate solution — the compiler already performs template type-checking and has all the information needed to emit this warning.


### Justification

This diagnostic fits the [extended diagnostics criteria](https://angular.dev/extended-diagnostics#new-diagnostics):

- **Common, non-obvious mistake**: Developers have no way to know a template binding or expression targets a deprecated symbol unless they hover over it in VS Code. This is especially problematic for inputs/outputs/models, which are completely invisible to existing lint tools.
- **The why is clear**: Deprecated symbols are typically removed in future versions, causing runtime breakage. Detecting them early reduces migration costs.
- **Clear solution**: The diagnostic message includes the replacement from the `@deprecated` JSDoc.
- **Low false-positive rate**: If a symbol is marked `@deprecated`, any usage is a true positive.
- **Applies to all Angular applications**: Any project consuming libraries or shared components with deprecated members benefits.
- **Improves program correctness**: Prevents future breakage during library/component upgrades.

### Proposed solution

Add a new **extended diagnostic** (e.g. `deprecatedSymbolInTemplate`) that emits a warning when a template references any `@deprecated` symbol.

The diagnostic should detect:

- Bindings to `@deprecated` inputs: `[inputName]="expr"`, `inputName="value"` (both signal `input()` and legacy `@Input()` decorator)
- Bindings to `@deprecated` outputs: `(outputName)="handler()"` (both `output()` and legacy `@Output()` decorator)
- Bindings to `@deprecated` models: `[(modelName)]="expr"` (two-way binding via `model()`)
- Usage of `@deprecated` components/directives via their selector: `<deprecated-cmp>`, `[deprecatedDirective]`
- Usage of `@deprecated` pipes in expressions: `{{ value | deprecatedPipe }}`
- Access to `@deprecated` public properties/methods in template expressions: `{{ obj.deprecatedProp }}`, `(click)="deprecatedMethod()"`
- Include the deprecation message from the JSDoc tag in the diagnostic message, so developers know the recommended replacement
- Be configurable as `warning` (default), `error`, or `suppress` via `angularCompilerOptions.extendedDiagnostics`, like all other extended diagnostics

Example diagnostic outputs:

```
warning NG81xx: The input 'icon' of component 'MyComponent' is deprecated: Use `iconUrl` instead.
warning NG81xx: The component 'DeprecatedComponent' is deprecated: Use `NewComponent` instead.
warning NG81xx: The pipe 'deprecatedPipe' is deprecated: Use `newPipe` instead.
warning NG81xx: The property 'items' of component 'MyComponent' is deprecated: Use `newItems()` instead.
```

### Alternatives considered

**Angular Language Service**: Detects all cases in the IDE (shows deprecated symbols as ~~strikethrough~~), but is not usable in CI. A possible alternative would be for the Language Service to expose a CLI or a `--diagnostics` mode that could report deprecated usages across a project, similar to how `tsc --noEmit` reports type errors. However, this would essentially duplicate the work of extended diagnostics, and integrating the check directly into the compiler keeps the toolchain simpler.
kept_issues.title: feat(compiler): add extended diagnostic for `@deprecated` symbols used in templates

Prior art and why now

This request was previously raised as 34605 (2020) and PR 34606, both closed as not_planned. The team's reasoning at the time was that they did not want to expand Angular's API surface further.

Several things have changed since that decision:

- NgOptimizedImage already manages elements internally — the directive emits hints for priority images. The Angular team has therefore already accepted programmatic management as a legitimate concern inside the framework; a shared, public service would make the same capability available to application code.
- Angular SSR (@angular/ssr) has become a first-class citizen. Managing canonical URLs, preconnect hints, and Web App Manifest links is now a standard SSR task that developers encounter on virtually every production Angular application.
- Incremental hydration and partial rendering (Angular v17+) increase the importance of and management in application code.
- A reference implementation is available as @grandgular/link, demonstrating a stable, well-tested API design that mirrors Meta and Title.

---

 Description

Angular ships Meta and Title as first-class services for managing document metadata, yet there is no equivalent for elements. Developers who need to manage canonical URLs, preload hints, stylesheets, or Web App Manifest links currently have to either:

- Manipulate the DOM directly (breaks Angular SSR)
- Reach for third-party libraries
- Write their own DOCUMENT + Renderer2 wrapper

A Link service would complete Angular's "document-head management" story.

---

 Describe the solution you'd like

 LinkDefinition

A type alias covering every standardised attribute of the HTML element, with an index signature for non-standard attributes. Deprecated HTML5 attributes (charset, rev, target) are kept for legacy compatibility, matching the approach taken by MetaDefinition which also retains deprecated fields.

 

 Link service

 

 Usage examples

 

---

 Placement

The service fits naturally inside the existing platform-browser package with no new entry points and no new peer dependencies:

 

---

 SSR compatibility

The proposed implementation uses Renderer2 (via RendererFactory2) and the DOCUMENT token exclusively. This is a deliberate improvement over the existing Meta service which relies on ɵDomAdapter (internal, unstable API): Renderer2 is public, integrates with custom/test renderers, and is consistent with how third-party Angular libraries are expected to interact with the DOM.

---

 Alternatives considered

- Extending NgOptimizedImage: too narrow in scope; canonical URLs and manifest links have nothing to do with images.
- Keeping it as a community library: the same argument could have been made against Meta and Title. Document-head management is a sufficiently common concern to warrant first-class framework support.
- Using @angular/platform-browser's DomAdapter directly: DomAdapter is marked ɵ (internal) and is not recommended for application or library use.

---

 Breaking changes

None. This is a purely additive change.

---

 Prior art / proof of concept

A reference implementation is published as @grandgular/link (source: It has been used in production applications and its test suite covers all public API methods, SSR rendering, deduplication, and edge cases.

Which @angular/ package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request?

@angular/forms/signals

 Description

With disabled(path, { when: myConditional });, I can disable a whole path under some condition.
However, I often have huge forms where I need to disable all but a few distinct fields under some condition.

Writing dozens of disabled(path.f1, { when: myConditional });, disabled(path.f2, { when: myConditional });, ... is not only cumbersome, but also requires me to remember that I need to add another disabled rule when I extend my form model by a new field.

I tried to implement my own allDisabledExcept function, but then noticed it to be less trivial than I thought, because the FieldPathNode proxies that I have to handle in such implementation seem to be for internal usage only.

(Sorry, if this has already been requested by other people and I did not find)

 Proposed solution

It would be nice to simply extend the existing disabled like so:
disabled(path, { when: myConditional, except: [path.f3.f3_2.f3_2_5, path.f3.f3_2.f3_2_6] });

 Alternatives considered

Implementing own allDisabledExcept function, but this does not seem to be trivial.

_common_

 Description

The Temporal API reached TC39 Stage 4 in March 2026 and is now part of ES2026. It's shipping natively in Firefox 139+, Chrome 144+, and Edge 144+, with Node.js 26+ enabling it unflagged, and TypeScript 6.0 ships built-in types under esnext.temporal. Safari currently only has partial support in Technology Preview, so it's clearly not yet a baseline that Angular could require but the trajectory suggests full cross-browser support isn't far off.

This isn't a request to ship full Temporal support in DatePipe today. It's a proposal to start thinking about the design now, so that when Safari catches up, Angular is ready to fully support it.

I'm happy to help with the design discussion and, if the proposal is accepted and the timing is appropriate, I'd also be interested in working on an implementation.

 Proposed solution

Open a discussion on how DatePipe would extend to accept Temporal.PlainDate, Temporal.PlainDateTime, Temporal.ZonedDateTime, and Temporal.Instant inputs.

 Alternatives considered

- Wait until Safari ships full support before discussing anything.
- A separate TemporalPipe or TemporalDatePipe.
- Leaving DatePipe as it is.

Which @angular/ package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request?

core

 Description

@HostListener supports global event targets such as document:, window: and body::

 

There is currently no equivalent target for the root node of the directive/component host element (hostElement.getRootNode()).

This becomes important for directives and components that can run both in the regular document and inside Shadow DOM. Listening on document is not equivalent to listening on the current root: when an element is rendered inside a ShadowRoot, the natural event scope can be that shadow root rather than the owner document.

Today this requires dropping the declarative @HostListener API and manually resolving the root and managing the listener lifecycle, for example:

 

 Proposed solution

Add a root: event target which resolves to getRootNode() of the host element:

 

Conceptually, Angular would resolve root: at directive/component creation time as:

 

This means:

- for a regular element in the document, the target is Document;
- for an element inside Shadow DOM, the target is its ShadowRoot.

It would make listeners naturally follow the DOM tree in which the host is actually rendered and would provide a declarative counterpart to manually calling getRootNode().addEventListener(...).

If the same event-target syntax is shared with template event bindings, supporting (root:click) there as well would also be useful and consistent.

 Alternatives considered

1. @HostListener('document:click')

This does not express the same semantics. A reusable directive should not have to know whether its host lives directly in Document or in a ShadowRoot.

2. Manual addEventListener / removeEventListener

This works, but requires resolving getRootNode(), retaining the listener reference, and handling destruction manually. It loses the concise declarative lifecycle management provided by @HostListener.

3. RxJS fromEvent(hostElement.getRootNode(), 'click')

This also works, but similarly requires imperative setup and teardown (takeUntilDestroyed, etc.) for something that otherwise maps naturally to @HostListener.

4. A custom EventManagerPlugin

Applications can implement their own event target syntax, but this is disproportionate for a standard DOM concept (Node.getRootNode()) and makes reusable libraries depend on application-level event manager configuration.

 Additional

If this approach is approved, I’d be happy to submit a PR with the implementation and tests.
kept_issues.title: Support `root:` event target in `@HostListener`

Feature Description

RouterTestingHarness exposes the navigateByUrl method, which only accepts a string.

I suggest adding a navigate method, similar to the one exposed by Router. This would allow passing initial configuration such as fragment and query params.

I would be willing to open a pull request to add the feature.

 Use Case

The navigate method already offers good ergonomics for handling fragments and query params, but has no equivalent in the testing utils.

In tests, configuring initial fragment or query params requires injecting the router and performing an additional navigation, which is unnecessary boilerplate and differs from how such navigations are handled in source code.

A new method would help avoid boilerplate code and facilitate the creation of a proper initial URL.
